blocks.text: If you count everyone with a stomach ache as a case, your outbreak might be ten times bigger than it really is. How should investigators decide who counts?

chunks.text: A **case definition** is a set of rules for who counts as a case: **person**, **place**, **time**, and **symptoms**. A broad definition finds more people but includes non-cases (low **specificity**). A narrow one is cleaner but misses real cases (low **sensitivity**).

An **epidemic curve** is a histogram of when people got sick. Its shape hints at the source: **point source** (one narrow peak), **continuous source** (a long plateau), or **propagated** spread (waves).

steps.caption: Point source: everyone exposed once, such as one meal. A single sharp peak.
Continuous source: exposure goes on, such as contaminated water. A long plateau.
Propagated: sick people infect others. Waves roughly one incubation period apart.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a curve
steps: Situation: A curve rises over two days, peaks, and then nearly disappears within four days.
Ask: how many exposures could cause that? Probably one event.
Ask: does it show waves? No.
Conclusion: this looks like a point source. The investigator should ask what almost everyone shared at one time.

bullets: A case definition uses person, place, time, and symptoms.
Too broad lowers specificity; too narrow lowers sensitivity.
Point source: one peak. Continuous source: plateau. Propagated: waves.
Curve shape helps narrow down the source.
